# 1 · Motivation

This document fits a multivariate Bayesian animal model to four *Nemophila
menziesii* populations (AC, BB, BO, HR) and uses the resulting **G** matrices
to characterise the genetic architecture of five focal traits — corolla
diameter, specific leaf area (SLA), δ¹³C, mean seed mass (msm), and
fecundity — and the selection acting on them.

It is a re-implementation of an earlier analysis that the manuscript review
flagged on a number of methodological points. The structure of this document
walks through each step of the analysis in the order in which it must be
executed, with a short explanation before each block of code.

The five biggest changes versus the original analysis are:

1. **Maternal (dam) random effect** — separates V_A from V_maternal in the
   paternal half-sib design.
2. **Block and within-block spatial random effects** — the field design has 3
   blocks per site; treating spatial structure as fixed factors blew up at BB
   (158 Locations × 5 traits ≈ 775 parameters for ~441 plants).
3. **Genetic selection gradient β_G** — computed from the posterior of **G**
   via the Robertson–Price identity, alongside the standard Lande–Arnold β_P.
4. **Full posterior propagation** — evolvability metrics, eigenanalysis, and
   Random Skewers are computed per draw, not on the posterior mean of **G**.
5. **Deterministic data cleaning** — no unseeded `sample()` calls; the
   F-plant substitution rule is fully reproducible.

The remainder is laid out as: setup → data → model → diagnostics → posterior
quantities → genetic correlations → eigenanalysis → evolvability → population
comparison → selection → viability → sensitivity analyses.

# 2 · Setup

## 2.1 Libraries and namespace hygiene

`evolqg` (for Random Skewers) loads `plyr`, which masks several `dplyr`
verbs. The `conflicted` package below forces `dplyr` to win whenever both
versions are on the search path.

```{r libs}
options(rgl.useNULL = TRUE)   # evolqg pulls in rgl; avoid X11 dependency

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tidyverse)
  library(here)
  library(MCMCglmm)
  library(nadiv)
  library(coda)
  library(evolqg)
  library(broom)
  library(patchwork)
  library(car)        # vif()
  library(sandwich)   # HC3 robust variance
  library(lmtest)     # coeftest / waldtest with vcov.
  library(multcompView) # compact letter displays from Tukey HSD
  library(ggh4x)        # per-facet scale overrides (δ¹³C y-axis inversion)
})

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(conflicted))
for (fn in c("mutate", "rename", "filter", "select", "summarise", "summarize",
             "arrange", "group_by", "ungroup", "transmute", "count", "tally",
             "distinct", "bind_rows", "bind_cols", "recode")) {
  try(conflicted::conflict_prefer(fn, "dplyr", quiet = TRUE), silent = TRUE)
}

set.seed(20260520)
```

## 2.2 Run-time configuration

`TEST_RUN <- TRUE` runs short MCMC chains (1–2 min total) for debugging.
Set to `FALSE` for the publication-quality fit; the difference is roughly
two orders of magnitude in run time.

```{r runtime-config}
TEST_RUN <- FALSE

if (TEST_RUN) {
  N_CHAINS <- 2
  NITT     <- 6000
  BURNIN   <- 1000
  THIN     <- 5
  N_SKEWERS <- 200
  N_POST_DRAWS_FOR_SKEWERS <- 100   # subsample posterior to speed up
} else {
  N_CHAINS <- 3
  NITT     <- 200000
  BURNIN   <- 20000
  THIN     <- 100
  N_SKEWERS <- 2000
  N_POST_DRAWS_FOR_SKEWERS <- 1000
}
```

## 2.2.1 Fit caching

The full-resolution MCMC fits take ~3–5 h on this machine. To make it
practical to re-knit just the downstream sections (β_G, plots, sensitivity)
without re-running MCMC, every fit is saved to `cache/` as an RDS file and
reloaded on subsequent knits. Set `FORCE_REFIT <- TRUE` to bypass the cache
(e.g. after changing the model formula or prior).

```{r fit-cache-setup}
FORCE_REFIT <- FALSE
CACHE_DIR   <- here::here("cache")
dir.create(CACHE_DIR, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

cache_fit <- function(name, expr) {
  fpath <- file.path(CACHE_DIR, paste0(name, ".rds"))
  if (!FORCE_REFIT && file.exists(fpath)) {
    message("Loading cached fit: ", name)
    return(readRDS(fpath))
  }
  message("Fitting (not cached): ", name)
  obj <- force(expr)
  saveRDS(obj, fpath)
  obj
}
```

## 2.3 Population configuration and trait list

Each population uses a slightly different field layout. AC has 10 seeds per
1-m segment and uses transects; BB has 8 seeds and uses 158 named
Locations; BO and HR each have 8 seeds and use transects. AC also includes
a watered-treatment block ("W") that is excluded from this analysis.

```{r pop-config}
POP_CONFIG <- list(
  AC = list(file = "data/AC_compiledsheet_full_2022.csv",
            spatial = "Transect", seeds_sown = 10, exclude_blocks = "W"),
  BB = list(file = "data/BB_compiledsheet_full_2022.csv",
            spatial = "Location", seeds_sown = 8,  exclude_blocks = "W"),
  BO = list(file = "data/BO_compiledsheet_full_2022.csv",
            spatial = "Transect", seeds_sown = 8,  exclude_blocks = "W"),
  HR = list(file = "data/HR_compiledsheet_full_2022.csv",
            spatial = "Transect", seeds_sown = 8,  exclude_blocks = "W")
)

TRAITS <- c("corolla_z", "SLA_z", "d13C_z", "msm_z", "fec_z")
NT     <- length(TRAITS)
```

When the Dryad package is still private, files placed in `data/` by hand

```{r fetch-data}
source(here::here("fetch_dryad.R"))
fetch_dryad(c("AC_compiledsheet_full_2022.csv",
```

# 3 · Data preparation

## 3.1 The per-population cleaning function

`prep_population()` does four things, in order:

1. **Normalises donor and recipient labels** so the same dam appears under
   one name in the pedigree (the raw sheets use mixed prefixes).
2. **Repairs the survival flag**. If a plant has `total_fruits > 0` but is
   marked `surv_to_flower == 0`, it clearly survived to flowering — flip it
   to 1. The `!is.na(total_fruits) &` guard keeps NAs as NAs (otherwise
   `ifelse(NA, …)` would silently turn recorded 0s into NAs).
3. **Builds a true segment key**: `paste(Block, Recipient, spatial_unit)`.
   Earlier versions used `ceiling(row_number() / 8)` to bin segments, which
   silently mixed AC segments together (AC has 10 seeds per segment, not 8).
   The current key is robust across populations.
4. **Picks the F-plant deterministically**. The original protocol designated
   one focal plant per segment for trait measurement, but if that plant
   died before flowering a sibling was substituted. We reproduce that rule
   by promoting the **first surviving sibling** in row order, and as a last
   resort the first row (which will then enter the model with W = 0).

The output is a list with `all` (all rows, used for the viability GLM) and
`fp` (F-plants only, used for the animal model).

```{r prep-fn}
prep_population <- function(pop_code, cfg) {
  fpath <- here::here(cfg[["file"]])
  raw <- readr::read_csv(fpath, show_col_types = FALSE)
  spatial <- cfg$spatial

  if (length(cfg$exclude_blocks) > 0) {
    raw <- raw %>% filter(!(Block %in% cfg$exclude_blocks))
  }

  raw <- raw %>%
    mutate(
      Donor     = paste0("Donor_",     pop_code, "_",
                         str_remove(Donor,
                                    paste0("^Donor_", pop_code, "_|^",
                                           pop_code, "_"))),
      Recipient = paste0("Recipient_", pop_code, "_",
                         str_remove(Recipient,
                                    paste0("^Recipient_", pop_code, "_|^",
                                           pop_code, "_"))),
      F_plant   = ifelse(F_plant == TRUE, 1L, 0L),
      F_plant   = ifelse(is.na(F_plant), 0L, F_plant),
      surv_to_flower = ifelse(!is.na(total_fruits) & total_fruits > 0 &
                                surv_to_flower == 0,
                              1, surv_to_flower)
    ) %>%
    rename(spatial_unit = !!sym(spatial)) %>%
    mutate(spatial_unit = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(spatial_unit))) %>%
    filter(!is.na(spatial_unit)) %>%
    mutate(
      sample_ID = str_c(Year, Donor, Recipient, Gen,
                        str_pad(spatial_unit, width = 3, pad = "0"),
                        Plant_ID, sep = "_"),
      sample_ID  = str_replace(sample_ID, "^([^_]*)_", "\\1-"),
      segment_id = paste(Block, Recipient, spatial_unit, sep = "_")
    )

  # Deterministic F_plant assignment: where no plant in a segment is flagged
  # as F_plant, take the first surviving sibling. If none survived, take the
  # first row (which will contribute W = 0 to the selection analysis).
  raw <- raw %>%
    group_by(segment_id) %>%
    mutate(
      seg_has_fplant = sum(F_plant) > 0,
      seg_first_surv = which(surv_to_flower == 1)[1],
      seg_pick_idx   = ifelse(!is.na(seg_first_surv), seg_first_surv, 1L),
      F_plant        = ifelse(!seg_has_fplant & row_number() == seg_pick_idx,
                              1L, F_plant)
    ) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    select(-seg_has_fplant, -seg_first_surv, -seg_pick_idx)

  # Segment-level survival count (number alive out of seeds_sown).
  raw <- raw %>%
    group_by(segment_id) %>%
    mutate(total_surv_to_flower = sum(surv_to_flower, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    ungroup()

  fp <- raw %>% filter(F_plant == 1L) %>%
    mutate(
      animal     = sample_ID,
      dam        = Recipient,
      sire       = Donor,
      block      = factor(Block),
      transect_f = factor(spatial_unit),
      corolla    = corolla_diam_mm_SEG,
      SLA        = SLA_SEG,
      d13C       = d13C_SEG,
      msm        = msm_all,
      fec        = est_fecundity,
      surv       = surv_to_flower
    )

  # Centre+scale to mean 0 / sd 1 (z-scaling).
  z <- function(x) {
    m <- mean(x, na.rm = TRUE); s <- sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
    if (!is.finite(s) || s == 0) return(rep(NA_real_, length(x)))
    (x - m) / s
  }
  fp <- fp %>%
    mutate(
      corolla_z = z(corolla),
      SLA_z     = z(SLA),
      d13C_z    = z(d13C),
      msm_z     = z(msm),
      fec_z     = z(fec)
    )

  list(all = raw, fp = fp, pop = pop_code, spatial = spatial)
}
```

## 3.2 Building the pedigree

`MCMCglmm` needs an inverse-relatedness matrix Aⁱⁿᵛ. We construct it
deterministically from the F-plants: each plant's parents are its `Donor`
(sire) and `Recipient` (dam); founder dams and sires that never appear as
offspring are added as parentless rows so the pedigree closes.

```{r prep-ped-fn}
build_pedigree <- function(fp) {
  ped <- tibble(
    animal = as.character(fp$sample_ID),
    dam    = fp$Recipient,
    sire   = fp$Donor
  )
  missing_parents <- setdiff(unique(c(ped$dam, ped$sire)), ped$animal)
  ped2 <- bind_rows(
    ped,
    tibble(animal = missing_parents,
           dam = NA_character_, sire = NA_character_)
  ) %>% distinct(animal, .keep_all = TRUE)
  ped_ord <- prepPed(as.data.frame(ped2))
  Ainv <- MCMCglmm::inverseA(ped_ord)$Ainv
  list(ped = ped_ord, Ainv = Ainv)
}
```

## 3.3 Run the cleaning across all four populations

```{r load-all}
pop_data <- purrr::map(names(POP_CONFIG),
                       ~ prep_population(.x, POP_CONFIG[[.x]]))
names(pop_data) <- names(POP_CONFIG)
```

## 3.4 Sample sizes

How many sown plants, F-plants, sires, dams, and blocks per population?
This table grounds every effective-sample-size discussion downstream — if
ESS looks low, look here first.

**Table 1.** Sample sizes per population. Columns report total sown
plants, survivors to flowering, F-plants entering the animal model,
number of unique sires (donors), dams (recipients), blocks, and
transects, per-trait observation counts, and the number of complete
cases across all five focal traits (corolla, SLA, δ¹³C, mean seed mass,
fecundity).

```{r sample-sizes}
sample_sizes <- purrr::map_dfr(pop_data, function(d) {
  fp <- d$fp
  tibble(
    Pop          = d$pop,
    n_sown       = nrow(d$all),
    n_survivors  = sum(d$all$surv_to_flower == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_fitness_plants = nrow(fp),
    n_sires      = length(unique(fp$sire)),
    n_dams       = length(unique(fp$dam)),
    n_blocks     = length(unique(fp$block)),
    n_spatial    = length(unique(fp$transect_f)),
    n_corolla    = sum(!is.na(fp$corolla_z)),
    n_SLA        = sum(!is.na(fp$SLA_z)),
    n_d13C       = sum(!is.na(fp$d13C_z)),
    n_msm        = sum(!is.na(fp$msm_z)),
    n_fec        = sum(!is.na(fp$fec_z)),
    n_complete_4traits_fec =
      sum(complete.cases(fp[, c("corolla_z", "SLA_z", "d13C_z",
                                "msm_z", "fec_z")]))
  )
})
sample_sizes
```

## 3.5 Missingness per trait

MCMCglmm imputes missing trait values under the joint multivariate Gaussian
likelihood (conditional on G, V_M, V_block, V_transect, V_R). Traits with
high missingness contribute correspondingly less direct information to G
and its derived quantities. Note especially BB (SLA ~69%, msm ~75%) and
BO (SLA ~49%, msm ~66%) — the BB section below has a dedicated trait-drop
sensitivity check.

**Table 2.** Per-trait missingness by population. `pct_missing` is the
fraction of F-plants with no measurement for that trait. MCMCglmm
imputes these values under the joint multivariate Gaussian likelihood;
high-missingness traits (BB SLA 69%, BB msm 75%, BO msm 66%) therefore
contribute less direct information to **G** than the column counts suggest.

```{r missingness-table}
missingness_tbl <- purrr::imap_dfr(pop_data, function(d, pop) {
  fp <- d$fp
  tibble(
    Pop         = pop,
    trait       = TRAITS,
    n_observed  = sapply(TRAITS, function(t) sum(!is.na(fp[[t]]))),
    n_missing   = sapply(TRAITS, function(t) sum(is.na(fp[[t]]))),
    pct_missing = round(100 * sapply(TRAITS,
                                     function(t) mean(is.na(fp[[t]]))), 1)
  )
})
missingness_tbl
```

Before standardising, glance at the raw-scale means. These mirror Figure 4
and Table S3 of the manuscript.

**Table 3.** Raw (un-standardised) trait means ± SE per population, with
per-trait sample size. Units: corolla diameter (mm), SLA (mm²/mg), δ¹³C
(‰), mean seed mass (mg), fecundity (filled seeds per plant).

```{r trait-means-table}
trait_means_tbl <- purrr::imap_dfr(pop_data, function(d, pop) {
  fp <- d$fp
  tibble(
    Pop  = pop,
    trait = c("corolla_diam_mm", "SLA", "d13C", "mean_seed_mass_mg",
              "fecundity"),
    mean = c(mean(fp$corolla, na.rm = TRUE),
             mean(fp$SLA,     na.rm = TRUE),
             mean(fp$d13C,    na.rm = TRUE),
             mean(fp$msm,     na.rm = TRUE),
             mean(fp$fec,     na.rm = TRUE)),
    se   = c(sd(fp$corolla, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(fp$corolla))),
             sd(fp$SLA,     na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(fp$SLA))),
             sd(fp$d13C,    na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(fp$d13C))),
             sd(fp$msm,     na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(fp$msm))),
             sd(fp$fec,     na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(fp$fec)))),
    n    = c(sum(!is.na(fp$corolla)), sum(!is.na(fp$SLA)),
             sum(!is.na(fp$d13C)),    sum(!is.na(fp$msm)),
             sum(!is.na(fp$fec)))
  )
})
trait_means_tbl
```

```{r trait-means-plot, fig.width=11, fig.height=3.5}
trait_lbl <- c(corolla_diam_mm   = "corolla diameter (mm)",
               SLA               = "SLA (mm^2/mg)",
               d13C              = "δ13C (‰)",
               mean_seed_mass_mg = "mean seed mass (mg)",
               fecundity         = "fecundity (filled seeds)")

# One-way ANOVA + Tukey HSD per trait on raw values, with compact letter
# display. Two populations sharing a letter do not differ at α = 0.05.
trait_raw_long <- purrr::imap_dfr(pop_data, function(d, pop) {
  fp <- d$fp
  tibble(Pop = pop,
         corolla_diam_mm   = fp$corolla,
         SLA               = fp$SLA,
         d13C              = fp$d13C,
         mean_seed_mass_mg = fp$msm,
         fecundity         = fp$fec)
}) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-Pop, names_to = "trait", values_to = "value") %>%
  filter(!is.na(value))

trait_letters <- trait_raw_long %>%
  group_by(trait) %>%
  group_modify(~ {
    mod   <- aov(value ~ Pop, data = .x)
    pvals <- TukeyHSD(mod)$Pop[, "p adj"]
    lets  <- multcompView::multcompLetters(pvals)$Letters
    # Order letters by population mean (ascending) so "a" is the lowest mean.
    pop_means <- .x %>% group_by(Pop) %>%
      summarise(m = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
      arrange(m)
    lets_ordered <- lets[pop_means$Pop]
    unique_lets  <- unique(unlist(strsplit(paste(lets_ordered, collapse = ""), "")))
    relabel      <- setNames(letters[seq_along(unique_lets)], unique_lets)
    tibble(Pop = names(lets_ordered),
           letter = vapply(lets_ordered, function(s) {
             paste(relabel[strsplit(s, "")[[1]]], collapse = "")
           }, character(1)))
  }) %>%
  ungroup()

plot_dat <- trait_means_tbl %>%
  left_join(trait_letters, by = c("Pop", "trait")) %>%
  group_by(trait) %>%
  mutate(
    panel_pad = 0.08 * (max(mean + se, na.rm = TRUE) -
                        min(mean - se, na.rm = TRUE)),
    # For δ¹³C the y-axis is reversed, so "above the bar" visually means
    # below in data-coordinates (i.e. *more negative*). Push letters down
    # past mean − se in that panel.
    letter_y  = if (trait[1] == "d13C") mean - se - panel_pad
                else                    mean + se + panel_pad
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(trait = factor(recode(trait, !!!trait_lbl),
                        levels = unname(trait_lbl)))

ggplot(plot_dat, aes(Pop, mean, fill = Pop)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.25) +
  geom_text(aes(y = letter_y, label = letter),
            size = 3.5, vjust = 0, fontface = "bold") +
  facet_wrap(~ trait, scales = "free_y", nrow = 1) +
  # Positional list: one entry per facet in the order set by
  # `levels = unname(trait_lbl)` — corolla, SLA, δ¹³C, msm, fec.
  ggh4x::facetted_pos_scales(
    y = list(NULL, NULL, scale_y_reverse(), NULL, NULL)
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean ± SE") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        strip.text = element_text(size = 9))
```

**Figure 1.** Raw-scale trait means ± SE per population, one panel per
trait. Letters above each bar are compact-letter-display annotations from
trait-wise one-way ANOVAs (`aov(trait ~ Pop)`) followed by Tukey HSD
pairwise comparisons at α = 0.05; populations sharing a letter within a
panel do not differ significantly. Letters are ordered by ascending
population mean within each trait, **except for the δ¹³C panel**, whose
y-axis is reversed so that more-negative values (lower carbon-isotope
discrimination, higher water-use efficiency) appear at the top; the
letter `a` in that panel therefore corresponds to AC (the most-negative
δ¹³C population). Y-axes are panel-specific (free scales). Mirrors Figure
4 / Table S3 of the manuscript.

# 4 · The animal model

## 4.1 Model structure

For each population we fit the same multivariate model:

$$
\mathbf{y} \;=\; \text{trait intercepts} \;+\; \mathbf{a} \;+\; \mathbf{m}
\;+\; \mathbf{b} \;+\; \mathbf{t} \;+\; \mathbf{e}
$$

with the following random-effect structure:

- `us(trait):animal` — additive genetic effects via the pedigree, giving
  the unstructured 5×5 V_A matrix (this is **G**).
- `us(trait):dam` — maternal/dam effects, separating V_A from V_maternal.
- `idh(trait):block` — between-block environmental variance (diagonal).
- `idh(trait):transect_f` — within-block spatial variance (diagonal).
- `us(trait):units` — residual covariance (the 5×5 R matrix).

The diagonal (`idh`) form for block and transect avoids estimating dozens
of off-diagonal nuisance covariances we have no use for.

All five traits — including fecundity — are modelled with a Gaussian
family on the within-population z-scale. Fecundity is biologically a
zero-inflated, right-skewed count, so the Gaussian likelihood is a
convenience choice that will attenuate V_A(fec) and Cov_A(z, fec)
relative to a Poisson or negative-binomial family. We test sensitivity
to this in §13.1 by refitting AC with `log1p(fec)` z-scored as the
fecundity column; a Poisson/NB animal model is left for future work
because it would also require revisiting the joint Gaussian imputation
of missing trait values that MCMCglmm uses for the other four traits.

## 4.2 Priors: parameter-expanded vs inverse-Wishart

Two priors are used:

- **PX (parameter-expanded)** — weakly informative on correlations; this is
  the default for the main analysis. `alpha.V = diag(NT) * 1000` lets the
  scale of V_A and V_M be effectively unbounded. Applied to all four G
  components (animal, dam, block, transect). With only 3 blocks per site
  the inverse-Gamma-like prior used previously (`nu = 0.002`) caused R̂ > 1.2
  for HR block components; the PX form removes that pathology without
  committing to high or low V_block.
- **IW (inverse-Wishart, V = I, ν = NT)** — the original analysis's prior,
  retained as a sensitivity check (see §13.3).

```{r mcmc-fn}
fit_animal_model <- function(prep, peds, prior_type = "px",
                             nitt = NITT, burnin = BURNIN, thin = THIN,
                             n_chains = N_CHAINS) {

  dat  <- as.data.frame(prep$fp)
  Ainv <- peds$Ainv

  dat$animal     <- factor(trimws(as.character(dat$animal)),
                           levels = rownames(Ainv))
  dat$animal     <- droplevels(dat$animal)
  dat$dam        <- factor(dat$dam)
  dat$block      <- factor(dat$block)
  dat$transect_f <- factor(dat$transect_f)

  if (prior_type == "px") {
    # Parameter expansion on every G component, including block and transect.
    # With 3 blocks per site, the inverse-Gamma-like (nu=0.002) prior on
    # V_block previously caused R-hat > 1.2 for HR block components. PX
    # widens the support without committing to a high or low variance,
    # which is what Gelman (2006) recommends for variance components with
    # few random-effect levels.
    prior <- list(
      G = list(
        G1 = list(V = diag(NT), nu = NT, alpha.mu = rep(0, NT),
                  alpha.V = diag(NT) * 1000),     # animal (V_A)
        G2 = list(V = diag(NT), nu = NT, alpha.mu = rep(0, NT),
                  alpha.V = diag(NT) * 1000),     # dam (V_M)
        G3 = list(V = diag(NT), nu = NT, alpha.mu = rep(0, NT),
                  alpha.V = diag(NT) * 1000),     # block (idh, PX)
        G4 = list(V = diag(NT), nu = NT, alpha.mu = rep(0, NT),
                  alpha.V = diag(NT) * 1000)      # transect (idh, PX)
      ),
      R = list(V = diag(NT), nu = NT)
    )
  } else if (prior_type == "iw") {
    prior <- list(
      G = list(
        G1 = list(V = diag(NT), nu = NT),
        G2 = list(V = diag(NT), nu = NT),
        G3 = list(V = diag(NT), nu = 0.002),
        G4 = list(V = diag(NT), nu = 0.002)
      ),
      R = list(V = diag(NT), nu = NT)
    )
  } else stop("unknown prior_type")

  fit_one <- function(seed) {
    set.seed(seed)
    MCMCglmm(
      fixed    = cbind(corolla_z, SLA_z, d13C_z, msm_z, fec_z) ~ trait - 1,
      random   = ~ us(trait):animal + us(trait):dam
                 + idh(trait):block + idh(trait):transect_f,
      rcov     = ~ us(trait):units,
      family   = rep("gaussian", NT),
      ginverse = list(animal = Ainv),
      data     = dat,
      prior    = prior,
      nitt     = nitt, burnin = burnin, thin = thin,
      verbose  = FALSE
    )
  }

  purrr::map(seq_len(n_chains), fit_one)
}
```

## 4.3 Build the per-population pedigrees

```{r build-peds}
peds_list <- purrr::map(pop_data, ~ build_pedigree(.x$fp))
```

## 4.4 Fit the main models (PX prior, all four populations)

```{r fit-main}
fits_main <- cache_fit("fits_main_px", {
  purrr::map2(pop_data, peds_list,
              ~ fit_animal_model(.x, .y, prior_type = "px"))
})
```

## 4.5 Fit sensitivity models with the IW prior

AC is our "reference" population (most complete data). BB has the thinnest
spatial structure (156 Locations with ~1–3 F-plants each) and highest
missingness, making it the population where the PX prior does the most
work. We refit both with the original IW prior so we can compare in §13.3.

```{r fit-iw-sensitivity}
fits_iw_AC <- cache_fit("fits_iw_AC",
  fit_animal_model(pop_data$AC, peds_list$AC, prior_type = "iw"))
fits_iw_BB <- cache_fit("fits_iw_BB",
  fit_animal_model(pop_data$BB, peds_list$BB, prior_type = "iw"))
```

# 5 · MCMC diagnostics

The earlier implementation only checked R̂ on the V_A diagonals (~12% of
monitored parameters). The off-diagonals of G, the maternal covariance
matrix, and the residual covariance matrix all drive downstream quantities
(r_A, β_G, eigenanalysis), and they typically mix worse than diagonals.
Here we diagnose **every** monitored parameter — fixed effects (`Sol`) plus
every entry of every variance/covariance component (`VCV`).

## 5.1 Gelman–Rubin R̂

R̂ > 1.1 is the conventional concern threshold; > 1.2 is bad mixing. With
`TEST_RUN = TRUE`, expect some R̂ above threshold simply because the chains
are short.

**Table 4.** Gelman–Rubin convergence diagnostic (R̂) across all Sol +
VCV parameters per population. `conv_health` summarises the count of
parameters with R̂ > 1.1 and > 1.2; the second printed table lists any
parameter with R̂ > 1.1. Under `TEST_RUN = FALSE` the target is all
parameters with R̂ < 1.1.

```{r convergence-rhat}
gelman_summary <- function(fits, label) {
  mc <- mcmc.list(lapply(fits,
                         function(f) as.mcmc(cbind(f$Sol, f$VCV))))
  gd <- gelman.diag(mc, multivariate = FALSE, autoburnin = FALSE)
  tibble(Pop = label,
         param = rownames(gd$psrf),
         psrf  = gd$psrf[, 1],
         upper = gd$psrf[, 2])
}

conv_tbl <- purrr::map2_dfr(fits_main, names(fits_main),
                            ~ gelman_summary(.x, .y))

conv_health <- conv_tbl %>%
  group_by(Pop) %>%
  summarise(
    n_params         = n(),
    max_psrf         = max(psrf, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_psrf_above_1_1 = sum(psrf > 1.1, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_psrf_above_1_2 = sum(psrf > 1.2, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
conv_health
conv_tbl %>% filter(psrf > 1.1) %>% arrange(desc(psrf))
```

## 5.2 Effective sample size

ESS < 100 means the chain is essentially uninformative for that parameter;
< 400 is borderline. With `TEST_RUN = FALSE`, the target is ≥ 1000 for V_A
diagonals and the leading r_A entries.

**Table 5.** Effective sample size (ESS) per parameter, summarised
per population. `ess_health` reports the minimum ESS and the count of
parameters with ESS < 100 (uninformative) or < 400 (borderline). The
second printed table lists the 20 lowest-ESS parameters.

```{r convergence-ess}
ess_summary <- function(fits, label) {
  combined <- as.mcmc(do.call(rbind,
                              lapply(fits,
                                     function(f) cbind(f$Sol, f$VCV))))
  ess <- effectiveSize(combined)
  tibble(Pop = label, param = names(ess), ESS = unname(ess))
}
ess_tbl <- purrr::map2_dfr(fits_main, names(fits_main),
                           ~ ess_summary(.x, .y))

ess_health <- ess_tbl %>%
  group_by(Pop) %>%
  summarise(
    n_params        = n(),
    min_ESS         = min(ESS, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_ESS_below_100 = sum(ESS < 100, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_ESS_below_400 = sum(ESS < 400, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
ess_health
ess_tbl %>% arrange(ESS) %>% head(20)
```

# 6 · Extracting posterior quantities

The fit object is a list of `MCMCglmm` chains. Everything downstream (r_A,
h², eigenanalysis, β_G, evolvability, Random Skewers) is computed from the
VCV columns, so the next few helpers shape those columns into arrays we
can index by trait pair and posterior draw.

## 6.1 Small numerical helpers

`safe_hpd()` returns a 95% HPD interval but tolerates NAs and tiny samples
gracefully. `cov2cor_mat()` converts a covariance matrix to a correlation
matrix without R's `cov2cor` warning machinery.

```{r helpers}
safe_hpd <- function(x, prob = 0.95) {
  x <- x[is.finite(x)]
  if (length(x) < 2) return(c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
  as.numeric(HPDinterval(as.mcmc(x), prob = prob))
}

cov2cor_mat <- function(S) {
  d <- sqrt(diag(S))
  S / (d %o% d)
}
```

## 6.2 Reshaping the VCV output into trait × trait arrays

`build_G_array()` takes the VCV matrix (rows = posterior draws, columns =
named like `traitA:traitB.animal`) and returns a 3-D array indexed as
`[draw, trait_i, trait_j]`. The `suffix` argument selects which variance
component to extract — `"animal"` for **G**, `"dam"` for the maternal
covariance, `"units"` for the residual covariance.

```{r vcv-helpers}
combine_VCV <- function(fits) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, function(f) as.matrix(f$VCV)))
}

build_G_array <- function(VCV, suffix = "animal") {
  Gcol <- function(t1, t2) paste0("trait", t1, ":trait", t2, ".", suffix)
  out <- array(NA_real_, dim = c(nrow(VCV), NT, NT),
               dimnames = list(NULL, TRAITS, TRAITS))
  for (i in seq_along(TRAITS)) for (j in seq_along(TRAITS)) {
    out[, i, j] <- VCV[, Gcol(TRAITS[i], TRAITS[j])]
  }
  out
}

posterior_summary_matrix <- function(arr) {
  mean_mat <- apply(arr, c(2, 3), mean)
  l95 <- apply(arr, c(2, 3), function(x) safe_hpd(x)[1])
  u95 <- apply(arr, c(2, 3), function(x) safe_hpd(x)[2])
  list(mean = mean_mat, l95 = l95, u95 = u95,
       sig  = (l95 > 0) | (u95 < 0))
}

rA_from_G <- function(G_arr) {
  out <- array(NA_real_, dim = dim(G_arr), dimnames = dimnames(G_arr))
  for (k in seq_len(dim(G_arr)[1])) out[k, , ] <- cov2cor_mat(G_arr[k, , ])
  out
}
```

## 6.3 Per-population extraction including h²

`extract_pop()` packages the per-population posterior into one list. h² is
computed *per draw* with the proper phenotypic-variance denominator:

$$
h^2_i \;=\; \frac{V_{A,i}}{V_{A,i} + V_{M,i} + V_{\text{block},i}
+ V_{\text{transect},i} + V_{R,i}}
$$

```{r extract-pop-fn}
extract_pop <- function(fits) {
  VCV <- combine_VCV(fits)
  G_array <- build_G_array(VCV, "animal")
  M_array <- build_G_array(VCV, "dam")
  R_array <- build_G_array(VCV, "units")
  rA_array <- rA_from_G(G_array)

  block_cols    <- grep("\\.block$",      colnames(VCV), value = TRUE)
  transect_cols <- grep("\\.transect_f$", colnames(VCV), value = TRUE)

  h2_array <- array(NA_real_, dim = c(nrow(VCV), NT),
                    dimnames = list(NULL, TRAITS))
  for (i in seq_along(TRAITS)) {
    Va <- G_array[, i, i]
    Vm <- M_array[, i, i]
    Vr <- R_array[, i, i]
    bcol <- grep(paste0("trait", TRAITS[i], "\\.block$"),
                 block_cols,    value = TRUE)
    tcol <- grep(paste0("trait", TRAITS[i], "\\.transect_f$"),
                 transect_cols, value = TRUE)
    Vb   <- if (length(bcol) == 1) VCV[, bcol] else 0
    Vt   <- if (length(tcol) == 1) VCV[, tcol] else 0
    h2_array[, i] <- Va / (Va + Vm + Vb + Vt + Vr)
  }

  list(
    VCV = VCV,
    G_array = G_array,
    M_array = M_array,
    R_array = R_array,
    rA_array = rA_array,
    h2_array = h2_array,
    G_summary  = posterior_summary_matrix(G_array),
    M_summary  = posterior_summary_matrix(M_array),
    rA_summary = posterior_summary_matrix(rA_array)
  )
}
```

## 6.4 Run the extraction on every population

```{r extract-all}
post_main <- purrr::map(fits_main, extract_pop)
```

## 6.5 V_A diagonals

**Table 6.** Additive genetic variance (V_A) diagonals of **G** per
population and trait. `Va_mean` is the posterior mean, `Va_l95` /
`Va_u95` are the 95% HPD bounds. Traits are on the z-scored within-
population scale, so V_A is dimensionless and comparable across traits
and populations.

```{r tbl-Va}
Va_tbl <- purrr::imap_dfr(post_main, function(p, pop) {
  tibble(
    Pop = pop, trait = TRAITS,
    Va_mean = diag(p$G_summary$mean),
    Va_l95  = diag(p$G_summary$l95),
    Va_u95  = diag(p$G_summary$u95)
  )
})
Va_tbl
```

## 6.6 V_M diagonals (maternal/dam variance)

V_M from `us(trait):dam` is the variance among dams — it captures
maternal genetic effects, maternal common-environment effects, and
seed-provisioning effects together, because the design has no grand-dam
replication that could separate them. Compare against V_A in the
previous table: if V_M is large for a trait, the original analysis
(which lacked a dam effect) was almost certainly partitioning some of
that maternal/dam variance into V_A. A large V_M does not, on its own,
imply heritable maternal effects.

**Table 7.** Maternal/dam variance (V_M) diagonals per population and
trait, with 95% HPD intervals. Compare against V_A in Table 6 — large
V_M flags traits where the previous (no-dam) animal model would have
absorbed maternal variance into V_A.

```{r tbl-Vm}
Vm_tbl <- purrr::imap_dfr(post_main, function(p, pop) {
  tibble(
    Pop = pop, trait = TRAITS,
    Vm_mean = diag(p$M_summary$mean),
    Vm_l95  = diag(p$M_summary$l95),
    Vm_u95  = diag(p$M_summary$u95)
  )
})
Vm_tbl
```

## 6.7 Narrow-sense heritability

**Table 8.** Narrow-sense heritability (*h*² = V_A / (V_A + V_M +
V_block + V_transect + V_R)) per population and trait, computed per
posterior draw. `h2_mean` is the posterior mean; `h2_l95` / `h2_u95`
are the 95% HPD bounds.

```{r tbl-h2}
h2_tbl <- purrr::imap_dfr(post_main, function(p, pop) {
  tibble(
    Pop   = pop, trait = TRAITS,
    h2_mean = colMeans(p$h2_array, na.rm = TRUE),
    h2_l95  = apply(p$h2_array, 2, function(x) safe_hpd(x)[1]),
    h2_u95  = apply(p$h2_array, 2, function(x) safe_hpd(x)[2])
  )
})
h2_tbl
```

# 7 · Genetic correlations (r_A)

Per-draw genetic correlations come from converting each posterior G to a
correlation matrix. The upper triangle gives one row per trait pair per
population; the `sig` flag marks pairs whose 95% HPD excludes zero.

## 7.1 Pairwise r_A table

**Table 9.** Pairwise additive genetic correlations (r_A) per
population. One row per upper-triangle trait pair. `rA_mean` is the
posterior mean of the per-draw correlation; `rA_l95` / `rA_u95` give
the 95% HPD interval; `sig = TRUE` flags pairs whose HPD excludes 0.

```{r rA-table}
rA_pairs_tbl <- purrr::imap_dfr(post_main, function(p, pop) {
  rA_arr <- p$rA_array
  ut <- which(upper.tri(diag(NT)), arr.ind = TRUE)
  purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(ut)), function(idx) {
    i <- ut[idx, 1]; j <- ut[idx, 2]
    x <- rA_arr[, i, j]
    h <- safe_hpd(x)
    tibble(Pop    = pop,
           trait1 = TRAITS[i],
           trait2 = TRAITS[j],
           rA_mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
           rA_l95  = h[1], rA_u95 = h[2],
           sig     = isTRUE(h[1] > 0) || isTRUE(h[2] < 0))
  })
})
rA_pairs_tbl
```

Same data, formatted as `"mean [l95, u95]"` with **bold** for HPDs that
exclude zero (matches the original Rmd table style):

**Table 10.** Pairwise r_A in wide trait-by-trait format. Each cell
shows `"mean [l95, u95]"`; **bold** entries are correlations whose 95%
HPD excludes zero. Matches the manuscript table layout.

```{r rA-table-formatted}
rA_pairs_tbl %>%
  mutate(
    label = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", rA_mean, rA_l95, rA_u95),
    label = ifelse(sig, paste0("**", label, "**"), label),
    trait1 = factor(trait1, levels = TRAITS),
    trait2 = factor(trait2, levels = TRAITS)
  ) %>%
  select(Pop, trait1, trait2, label) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = trait2, values_from = label)
```

Cells whose 95% HPD excludes zero are bordered in black and shown at full

**Figure 2.** Pairwise additive genetic correlation (r_A) heatmaps, one

# 8 · Eigenanalysis of G

The eigendecomposition of G summarises which directions in trait space
hold most additive genetic variance. We work per draw so HPDs reflect
genuine posterior uncertainty.

## 8.1 Per-draw eigendecomposition

Eigenvectors flip sign arbitrarily between draws, so within each
population we sign-align each draw's eigenvector to the corresponding
eigenvector of the posterior-mean G before averaging.

```{r eigen-fn}
eigen_per_draw <- function(G_array) {
  niter <- dim(G_array)[1]
  G_mean <- apply(G_array, c(2, 3), mean)
  ref_vec <- eigen(G_mean, symmetric = TRUE)$vectors

  trace_vec <- numeric(niter)
  eigvals   <- matrix(NA_real_, niter, NT)
  prop_pc1  <- numeric(niter)
  prop_pc2  <- numeric(niter)
  loadings  <- array(NA_real_, dim = c(niter, NT, NT),
                     dimnames = list(NULL, TRAITS, paste0("PC", 1:NT)))
  for (k in seq_len(niter)) {
    Gk <- G_array[k, , ]
    ek <- eigen(Gk, symmetric = TRUE)
    trace_vec[k] <- sum(diag(Gk))
    eigvals[k, ] <- ek$values
    prop_pc1[k]  <- ek$values[1] / sum(ek$values)
    prop_pc2[k]  <- ek$values[2] / sum(ek$values)
    V <- ek$vectors
    for (j in seq_len(NT)) {
      if (sum(V[, j] * ref_vec[, j]) < 0) V[, j] <- -V[, j]
    }
    loadings[k, , ] <- V
  }
  list(trace = trace_vec, eigvals = eigvals,
       prop_pc1 = prop_pc1, prop_pc2 = prop_pc2, loadings = loadings)
}

eig_results <- purrr::map(post_main, ~ eigen_per_draw(.x$G_array))
```

## 8.2 Eigenvalue summary (Table 5 / S9 analogue)

Per population: trace(G), λ₁ … λ₅, and the proportion of variance on PC1
and PC2.

**Table 11.** Eigenvalue summary of **G** per population: posterior
mean of trace(**G**) (total genetic variance), eigenvalues λ₁–λ₅ with
95% HPD intervals (λ₁–λ₃ shown with HPDs; λ₄, λ₅ as means only), and
the proportion of variance on PC1 and PC2 with HPDs. Per-draw
quantities so HPDs reflect posterior uncertainty in **G**.

```{r eigen-summary-table}
eig_summary_tbl <- purrr::imap_dfr(eig_results, function(e, pop) {
  lam_hpd <- apply(e$eigvals, 2, safe_hpd)
  tibble(
    Pop          = pop,
    trace_mean   = mean(e$trace, na.rm = TRUE),
    trace_l95    = safe_hpd(e$trace)[1],
    trace_u95    = safe_hpd(e$trace)[2],
    lambda1_mean = mean(e$eigvals[, 1], na.rm = TRUE),
    lambda1_l95  = lam_hpd[1, 1], lambda1_u95 = lam_hpd[2, 1],
    lambda2_mean = mean(e$eigvals[, 2], na.rm = TRUE),
    lambda2_l95  = lam_hpd[1, 2], lambda2_u95 = lam_hpd[2, 2],
    lambda3_mean = mean(e$eigvals[, 3], na.rm = TRUE),
    lambda3_l95  = lam_hpd[1, 3], lambda3_u95 = lam_hpd[2, 3],
    lambda4_mean = mean(e$eigvals[, 4], na.rm = TRUE),
    lambda5_mean = mean(e$eigvals[, 5], na.rm = TRUE),
    prop_PC1_mean = mean(e$prop_pc1, na.rm = TRUE),
    prop_PC1_l95  = safe_hpd(e$prop_pc1)[1],
    prop_PC1_u95  = safe_hpd(e$prop_pc1)[2],
    prop_PC2_mean = mean(e$prop_pc2, na.rm = TRUE),
    prop_PC2_l95  = safe_hpd(e$prop_pc2)[1],
    prop_PC2_u95  = safe_hpd(e$prop_pc2)[2]
  )
})
eig_summary_tbl
```

## 8.3 PC2 reliability check

PC1 is almost always well separated from PC2 by eigenvalue magnitude, but
PC2 vs PC3 may not be — and when their HPDs overlap, sign-alignment is no
longer enough to stabilise their eigenvectors across draws. The averaged
loadings then pull toward the reference and understate uncertainty. This
chunk flags any population where λ₂ and λ₃ HPDs overlap so PC2 results
can be suppressed or caveated in the manuscript.

**Table 12.** PC2 reliability check per population. `pc2_reliable` is
TRUE if the 95% HPD for λ₂ does not overlap the HPD for λ₃; when FALSE,
PC2 eigenvectors are not stably identified across draws and the
averaged PC2 loadings should not be interpreted.

```{r pc2-reliable}
pc2_reliable_tbl <- eig_summary_tbl %>%
  mutate(
    pc2_reliable = lambda2_l95 > lambda3_u95,
    overlap_note = ifelse(pc2_reliable,
                          "λ₂ and λ₃ HPDs do not overlap — PC2 loadings stable",
                          "λ₂ and λ₃ HPDs OVERLAP — PC2 loadings unreliable")
  ) %>%
  select(Pop, lambda2_mean, lambda2_l95, lambda2_u95,
         lambda3_mean, lambda3_l95, lambda3_u95,
         pc2_reliable, overlap_note)
pc2_reliable_tbl
```

## 8.4 PC1 trait loadings

**Table 13.** PC1 trait loadings per population, with 95% HPD bounds
from per-draw sign-aligned eigenvectors. `main_contributor` flags
traits with |loading| > 0.2.

```{r pc1-loadings}
pc1_loadings_tbl <- purrr::imap_dfr(eig_results, function(e, pop) {
  pc1 <- e$loadings[, , 1]
  hp  <- apply(pc1, 2, safe_hpd)
  tibble(
    Pop   = pop,
    trait = TRAITS,
    loading_mean = colMeans(pc1, na.rm = TRUE),
    loading_l95  = hp[1, ],
    loading_u95  = hp[2, ],
    main_contributor = abs(colMeans(pc1, na.rm = TRUE)) > 0.2
  )
})
pc1_loadings_tbl
```

## 8.5 PC2 trait loadings (caveated for unreliable populations)

**Table 14.** PC2 trait loadings per population, with HPD bounds and
the `pc2_reliable` flag from Table 12. Loadings for populations with
`pc2_reliable = FALSE` are reported but should not be interpreted —
λ₂/λ₃ overlap means PC2 eigenvectors are not stably identified across
draws.

```{r pc2-loadings}
pc2_loadings_tbl <- purrr::imap_dfr(eig_results, function(e, pop) {
  pc2 <- e$loadings[, , 2]
  hp  <- apply(pc2, 2, safe_hpd)
  tibble(
    Pop   = pop,
    trait = TRAITS,
    loading_mean = colMeans(pc2, na.rm = TRUE),
    loading_l95  = hp[1, ],
    loading_u95  = hp[2, ],
    main_contributor = abs(colMeans(pc2, na.rm = TRUE)) > 0.2
  )
}) %>%
  left_join(pc2_reliable_tbl %>% select(Pop, pc2_reliable), by = "Pop")
pc2_loadings_tbl

unreliable_pops <- pc2_reliable_tbl %>%
  filter(!pc2_reliable) %>%
  pull(Pop)
if (length(unreliable_pops) > 0)
  message("PC2 loadings are unreliable for: ",
          paste(unreliable_pops, collapse = ", "),
          " (λ₂ and λ₃ HPDs overlap). ",
          "Suppress or caveat PC2 results for these populations.")
```

## 8.6 Compact contributor strings (manuscript table format)

A trait counts as a "main contributor" to a PC if `|loading| > 0.2`. We
also flag whether the PC is **reliable** at each population: a PC's
loadings are considered reliable only if at least one trait loading
has a 95% HPD that excludes zero. PC1 at AC, BB and BO has wide enough
loading HPDs that no individual loading excludes zero, so the
contributor strings for those populations should be read as posterior
means of an underdetermined eigenvector rather than as resolved trait
contributions. Only HR PC1 (d13C and msm both with HPDs excluding 0)
is loading-reliable. PC2 reliability is also flagged via the λ₂/λ₃
overlap criterion from Table 12 (unreliable at all four populations).

**Table 15.** Compact string summary of PC1 (`pc1_contrib_str`) and
PC2 (`pc2_contrib_str`) main contributors per population, in the
manuscript table format. A trait is listed if |loading| > 0.2 with the
sign of its mean loading. The `pc1_reliable` / `pc2_reliable` columns
flag whether the PC is interpretable at that population
(`pc1_reliable = TRUE` iff ≥ 1 PC1 loading HPD excludes 0;
`pc2_reliable` from Table 12).

```{r pc-contributor-strings}
make_contrib_str <- function(loadings_tbl) {
  loadings_tbl %>%
    filter(main_contributor) %>%
    mutate(sign  = ifelse(loading_mean > 0, "+", "−"),
           label = sprintf("%s (%s)",
                           recode(trait,
                                  corolla_z = "corolla",
                                  SLA_z     = "SLA",
                                  d13C_z    = "δ13C",
                                  msm_z     = "seed mass",
                                  fec_z     = "fecundity"),
                           sign)) %>%
    group_by(Pop) %>%
    summarise(contributors = paste(label, collapse = ", "),
              .groups = "drop")
}

pc1_reliable_tbl <- pc1_loadings_tbl %>%
  group_by(Pop) %>%
  summarise(pc1_reliable = any((loading_l95 > 0) | (loading_u95 < 0),
                               na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

pc1_contrib_str <- make_contrib_str(pc1_loadings_tbl) %>%
  rename(main_PC1_contributors = contributors) %>%
  left_join(pc1_reliable_tbl, by = "Pop")
pc1_contrib_str

pc2_contrib_str <- make_contrib_str(pc2_loadings_tbl) %>%
  rename(main_PC2_contributors = contributors) %>%
  left_join(pc2_reliable_tbl %>% select(Pop, pc2_reliable), by = "Pop")
pc2_contrib_str
```

# 9 · Evolvability metrics

For a unit vector **β** in trait space, the *evolvability* of G in
direction **β** is

$$
e(\boldsymbol{\beta}) \;=\; \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top} \mathbf{G}
\boldsymbol{\beta}
$$

i.e. the additive genetic variance projected onto **β**. Three summaries
across many random unit vectors are useful:

- **`e_mean`** — average evolvability (mean of e(**β**) over directions).
- **`e_min`** — evolvability in the *most-constrained* direction (the
  worst-case selection axis). Approaches λ_min(**G**) as the number of
  random vectors increases.
- **`e_max`** — evolvability in the *least-constrained* direction (the
  best-case selection axis). Approaches λ_max(**G**).
- **`c_mean`** — conditional evolvability, the variance in **β** that
  remains when all other axes are held fixed. Lower than `e_mean` whenever
  there are genetic constraints.
- **`a_mean`** — autonomy `c / e`. 1 means no constraint; near 0 means
  every direction is strongly constrained by correlations with other traits.

The ratio **`e_max / e_min`** is a scale-free index of multivariate
anisotropy in **G** — a value near 1 means G is roughly spherical (no
preferred direction of evolutionary response); a large ratio means G
is highly anisotropic and selection responses depend strongly on
direction.

We compute these per posterior draw using a fixed set of `N_SKEWERS`
random unit vectors **B**.

## 9.1 Per-draw computation

**Table 16.** Evolvability metrics per population in long format.
`e_mean` = average evolvability β'**G**β over `N_SKEWERS` random unit
vectors; `c_mean` = conditional evolvability (1 / β'**G**⁻¹β); `a_mean`
= autonomy c/e (1 = no constraint, 0 = fully constrained); `e_min`,
`e_max` = range of e(β) across direction vectors. Computed per
posterior draw; `l95`, `u95` are 95% HPD bounds.

```{r evolvability-fn}
rand_unit_vecs <- function(p, nvec) {
  M <- matrix(rnorm(nvec * p), nvec, p)
  M / sqrt(rowSums(M^2))
}

evolv_one <- function(G, B) {
  e <- rowSums((B %*% G) * B)
  cev <- tryCatch({
    Ginv <- solve(G)
    1 / rowSums((B %*% Ginv) * B)
  }, error = function(e) rep(NA_real_, nrow(B)))
  a <- cev / e
  c(e_mean = mean(e, na.rm = TRUE),
    e_min  = min(e,  na.rm = TRUE),
    e_max  = max(e,  na.rm = TRUE),
    c_mean = mean(cev, na.rm = TRUE),
    a_mean = mean(a,   na.rm = TRUE))
}

set.seed(20260520)
B <- rand_unit_vecs(NT, N_SKEWERS)

evol_tbl <- purrr::imap_dfr(post_main, function(p, pop) {
  niter <- dim(p$G_array)[1]
  m <- t(sapply(seq_len(niter),
                function(k) evolv_one(p$G_array[k, , ], B)))
  m <- as.data.frame(m)
  purrr::imap_dfr(m, function(x, metric) {
    h <- safe_hpd(x)
    tibble(Pop = pop, metric = metric,
           mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
           l95 = h[1], u95 = h[2])
  })
})
evol_tbl
```

### 9.1.1 Wide-format summary (manuscript table)

**Table 16b.** Evolvability metrics per population in wide format with
the anisotropy ratio `e_max / e_min`. Each cell is "posterior mean
[95% HPD lower, upper]".

```{r evolvability-wide-table}
fmt_mh <- function(mean, l95, u95)
  sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", mean, l95, u95)

evol_wide_tbl <- evol_tbl %>%
  mutate(cell = fmt_mh(mean, l95, u95)) %>%
  select(Pop, metric, cell, mean) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = metric,
              values_from = c(cell, mean),
              names_glue = "{metric}_{.value}") %>%
  mutate(
    anisotropy_ratio = round(e_max_mean / e_min_mean, 1)
  ) %>%
  select(Pop,
         e_mean = e_mean_cell,
         e_min  = e_min_cell,
         e_max  = e_max_cell,
         c_mean = c_mean_cell,
         a_mean = a_mean_cell,
         anisotropy_ratio)
evol_wide_tbl
```

**Figure 3.** Evolvability metrics by population. (A) Mean evolvability
e(β) = β'**G**β averaged over random unit vectors. (B) Conditional
evolvability c(β) = 1 / β'**G**⁻¹β. (C) Autonomy a = c/e. Points are
