# 10 · Population comparison via Random Skewers

The Random Skewers metric `r_RS` measures how similarly two **G**
matrices respond to random selection vectors: r_RS = 1 means identical
response, r_RS = 0 means orthogonal. We propagate posterior uncertainty
by drawing one posterior sample from each of the two populations per
comparison (rather than comparing only the posterior means).

**Power note.** With these data the Random Skewers HPDs span roughly
[0.15, 0.87] for every pairwise comparison (Table 17), so the metric
cannot distinguish "similar **G**" from "weakly correlated **G**" — both
are inside every HPD. The point estimates (r_RS ≈ 0.50–0.63) and the
permutation p-values from `evolqg::RandomSkewers()` (p_mean ≈ 0.10–0.17,
max ≈ 0.50) provide no statistical evidence that any pair of **G**
matrices is more or less similar than any other pair. We report the
metric for completeness but do not draw conclusions about
**G**-matrix divergence from these comparisons.

**Table 17.** Random Skewers comparison of **G** matrices between all
pairs of populations. `r_RS_mean` is the posterior mean of the response
correlation across `N_POST_DRAWS_FOR_SKEWERS` paired posterior draws,
each evaluated against `N_SKEWERS` random unit vectors. `r_RS_l95` /
`r_RS_u95` are 95% HPD bounds; `p_mean` / `p_max` are the mean and
maximum across-draw permutation p-values from
`evolqg::RandomSkewers()`.

```{r random-skewers}
# evolqg::RandomSkewers() returns a named numeric c(correlation, probability)
# when called on a pair of matrices — NOT c(correlation, pvalue). The earlier
# version pulled res["pvalue"], which is always NA, so the rs_tbl p-value
# columns came out as NaN / -Inf. Fixed below.
posterior_skewers <- function(G_array_1, G_array_2,
                              n_draws = N_POST_DRAWS_FOR_SKEWERS,
                              n_skewers = N_SKEWERS) {
  i1 <- sample(seq_len(dim(G_array_1)[1]), n_draws, replace = TRUE)
  i2 <- sample(seq_len(dim(G_array_2)[1]), n_draws, replace = TRUE)
  out <- vapply(seq_len(n_draws), function(k) {
    res <- tryCatch(
      RandomSkewers(G_array_1[i1[k], , ], G_array_2[i2[k], , ],
                    num.vectors = n_skewers),
      error = function(e) c(correlation = NA_real_, probability = NA_real_))
    c(correlation = unname(res["correlation"]),
      probability = unname(res["probability"]))
  }, numeric(2))
  t(out)
}

pop_names <- names(post_main)
pairs <- combn(pop_names, 2, simplify = FALSE)
rs_tbl <- purrr::map_dfr(pairs, function(pp) {
  rs <- posterior_skewers(post_main[[pp[1]]]$G_array,
                          post_main[[pp[2]]]$G_array)
  r <- rs[, "correlation"]
  p <- rs[, "probability"]
  h <- safe_hpd(r)
  tibble(pop1 = pp[1], pop2 = pp[2],
         r_RS_mean = mean(r, na.rm = TRUE),
         r_RS_sd   = sd(r,   na.rm = TRUE),
         r_RS_l95  = h[1], r_RS_u95 = h[2],
         p_mean    = mean(p, na.rm = TRUE),
         p_max     = suppressWarnings(max(p, na.rm = TRUE)))
})
rs_tbl
```

# 11 · Selection — phenotypic vs genetic gradients

The central added analysis: comparing the **phenotypic** selection
gradient β_P (the Lande–Arnold OLS regression) against the **genetic**
selection gradient β_G computed from **G** via the Robertson–Price
identity.

## 11.1 Lande–Arnold β_P (phenotypic)

Lande–Arnold's β_P is just the OLS regression of relative fitness on
standardised traits. Two adjustments to the textbook version are worth
calling out:

- **Relative-fitness denominator**: `w_rel = W / mean(W)`. Earlier
  iterations used `mean(W[W > 0 | surv == 1])`, which made `mean(w_rel)`
  not equal to 1 and gave an asymmetric estimator.
- **HC3 sandwich SEs**: residual variance in `w_rel` scales with fitness
  magnitude (a zero-inflated outcome guarantees heteroscedasticity), so
  the conventional OLS SEs are wrong. We use HC3 sandwich SEs and a
  HC3-based Wald test for the global F.

```{r beta-pheno-fn}
beta_pheno <- function(prep, total_fitness = FALSE) {
  d <- prep$fp %>%
    mutate(W = if (total_fitness) {
                  ifelse(surv == 1, ifelse(is.na(fec), 0, fec), 0)
              } else {
                  ifelse(is.na(fec), 0, fec)
              }) %>%
    select(corolla_z, SLA_z, d13C_z, msm_z, W) %>%
    drop_na()
  if (nrow(d) < 10) return(NULL)
  d$w_rel <- d$W / mean(d$W, na.rm = TRUE)
  mod <- lm(w_rel ~ corolla_z + SLA_z + d13C_z + msm_z, data = d)
  vifs <- tryCatch(car::vif(mod), error = function(e) rep(NA_real_, 4))
  vif_df <- tibble(term = names(vifs), vif = unname(vifs))
  V_HC3 <- sandwich::vcovHC(mod, type = "HC3")
  ct    <- lmtest::coeftest(mod, vcov. = V_HC3)
  wt    <- lmtest::waldtest(mod, vcov = V_HC3)
  q     <- qt(0.975, df.residual(mod))
  coefs <- tibble(
    term      = rownames(ct),
    estimate  = ct[, "Estimate"],
    std.error = ct[, "Std. Error"],
    statistic = ct[, "t value"],
    p.value   = ct[, "Pr(>|t|)"],
    conf.low  = ct[, "Estimate"] - q * ct[, "Std. Error"],
    conf.high = ct[, "Estimate"] + q * ct[, "Std. Error"],
    n         = nrow(d)
  ) %>%
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
    left_join(vif_df, by = "term")
  g <- broom::glance(mod) %>%
    select(r.squared, adj.r.squared, df, df.residual, nobs) %>%
    mutate(F_HC3 = wt$F[2], p_HC3 = wt$`Pr(>F)`[2])
  attr(coefs, "model_fit") <- g
  coefs
}
```

### 11.1.1 Fecundity-only β_P (the classic Lande–Arnold)

**Table 18.** Phenotypic selection gradients β_P (fecundity-only
relative fitness) per population and trait, from OLS regression of
`w_rel = fec / mean(fec)` on z-scored corolla, SLA, δ¹³C, and msm
across complete-case rows. `std.error`, `statistic`, `p.value`, and
`conf.low`/`conf.high` use HC3 sandwich SEs; `n` is the per-population
complete-case sample size; `vif` is the variance inflation factor for
each predictor.

```{r beta-P-fec}
beta_P_tbl <- purrr::imap_dfr(pop_data, function(prep, pop) {
  beta_pheno(prep, total_fitness = FALSE) %>%
    mutate(Pop = pop, fitness_def = "fec_only_flowering", .before = 1)
})
beta_P_tbl
```

### 11.1.2 Total-fitness β_P (survival × fecundity)

In this dataset non-survivors don't have trait measurements, so the
fec-only and survival × fec regression samples are nearly identical. The
total-fitness column matters more in datasets where some non-survivors
were measured pre-mortality.

**Table 19.** Phenotypic selection gradients β_P using total fitness
(survival × fecundity, with non-survivors = 0) as the fitness
denominator. `beta_P_all` combines this table with Table 19 for direct
side-by-side comparison with Table 18. In this dataset the fec-only
and total-fitness samples nearly coincide because non-survivors have
no trait data.

```{r beta-P-total}
beta_P_total <- purrr::imap_dfr(pop_data, function(prep, pop) {
  beta_pheno(prep, total_fitness = TRUE) %>%
    mutate(Pop = pop, fitness_def = "surv_x_fec", .before = 1)
})
beta_P_all <- bind_rows(beta_P_tbl, beta_P_total)
beta_P_all
```

### 11.1.3 Fit summary

R², F (HC3), p (HC3), n, and max VIF for the fecundity-only regressions.
This is what the manuscript text "R² ≈ 0.10, all VIF < 1.1" comes from.

**Table 20.** Lande–Arnold β_P fit summary per population for the
fecundity-only regression: R² and adjusted R², HC3-based global F and
its p-value, residual degrees of freedom, complete-case n, and the
maximum VIF across the four trait predictors.

```{r beta-P-fit-summary}
beta_P_fit_summary <- purrr::imap_dfr(pop_data, function(prep, pop) {
  coefs <- beta_pheno(prep, total_fitness = FALSE)
  if (is.null(coefs)) return(NULL)
  g <- attr(coefs, "model_fit")
  tibble(Pop = pop,
         r_squared     = g$r.squared,
         adj_r_squared = g$adj.r.squared,
         F_HC3         = g$F_HC3,
         p_HC3         = g$p_HC3,
         df_resid      = g$df.residual,
         n             = g$nobs,
         max_vif       = max(coefs$vif, na.rm = TRUE))
})
beta_P_fit_summary
```

## 11.2 Robertson–Price β_G (genetic)

For non-fitness traits **z** and fitness trait *w*,

$$
\boldsymbol{\beta}_G \;=\; \mathbf{G}_{zz}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Cov}_A(z, w)
$$

computed draw by draw to propagate posterior uncertainty.

**Scale and likelihood notes.**

1. *Scale (rescaled to the Lande w_rel form).* The animal model fits G
   on z-scored fecundity (`fec_z`), so the off-diagonal column of G
   directly yields Cov_A(z, z_fec). Lande's equation Δz̄ = G β requires
   β = G_zz⁻¹·Cov_A(z, w_rel), where w_rel = W / W̄. Because
   w_rel = 1 + CV(W) · z_fec (with CV(W) = SD(W) / mean(W) on the raw
   scale), Cov_A(z, w_rel) = CV(W) · Cov_A(z, z_fec). We therefore
   multiply each per-draw β_G by CV(fec) per population — a deterministic
   rescaling, so HPD widths scale proportionally. β_G is now on the
   relative-fitness scale and directly comparable to the Lande–Arnold
   β_P.

2. *Gaussian likelihood on count data*: fecundity is a non-negative,
   right-skewed integer. The Gaussian likelihood attenuates V_A(fec) and
   Cov_A(z, fec) relative to a Poisson or negative-binomial likelihood,
   and β_G with it. The `log1p(fec)` sensitivity check in §13.1 gauges
   whether this attenuation matters in practice.

**Table 21.** Genetic selection gradients β_G per population and trait,
from the Robertson–Price identity β_G = **G**_zz⁻¹ Cov_A(z, w_rel)
computed draw by draw and rescaled to the relative-fitness scale by
multiplying each draw by `cv_fec = SD(fec)/mean(fec)` per population
(see §11.2). `beta_G_median` is the posterior median (robust to
heavy-tailed posteriors); `beta_G_mean` is reported only for diagnostic
comparison. `beta_G_l95`/`beta_G_u95` are 95% HPD bounds.
`n_kept`/`n_dropped` count posterior draws retained vs excluded because
**G**_zz was numerically near-singular (`rcond < 1e-10`); in practice
`n_dropped` is ~0 because the threshold is strict, and the heavy tails
that matter for the mean/median gap come from finite but
ill-conditioned draws rather than from singular ones. `sig = TRUE`
flags HPDs that exclude zero.

```{r beta-genetic-fn}
beta_genetic_posterior <- function(G_array, fec_index = 5,
                                   cv_factor = 1,
                                   rcond_threshold = 1e-10) {
  # cv_factor: SD(fitness)/mean(fitness) on the raw scale. Converts
  # G_zz^{-1} Cov_A(z, z_fec) → G_zz^{-1} Cov_A(z, w_rel), since
  # w_rel = 1 + cv_factor * z_fec implies Cov_A(z, w_rel) = cv_factor *
  # Cov_A(z, z_fec). Set cv_factor = 1 to retain the z-scale output.
  z_idx <- setdiff(seq_len(NT), fec_index)
  niter <- dim(G_array)[1]
  out   <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = niter, ncol = length(z_idx),
                  dimnames = list(NULL, TRAITS[z_idx]))
  n_dropped_rcond <- 0L
  n_dropped_solve <- 0L
  for (k in seq_len(niter)) {
    Gk    <- G_array[k, , ]
    G_zz  <- Gk[z_idx, z_idx]
    G_zw  <- Gk[z_idx, fec_index]
    if (!is.finite(rcond(G_zz)) || rcond(G_zz) < rcond_threshold) {
      n_dropped_rcond <- n_dropped_rcond + 1L
      next
    }
    out[k, ] <- tryCatch(
      cv_factor * as.numeric(solve(G_zz, G_zw)),
      error = function(e) {
        n_dropped_solve <<- n_dropped_solve + 1L
        rep(NA_real_, length(z_idx))
      }
    )
  }
  attr(out, "n_total")         <- niter
  attr(out, "n_dropped_rcond") <- n_dropped_rcond
  attr(out, "n_dropped_solve") <- n_dropped_solve
  attr(out, "n_kept")          <- niter - n_dropped_rcond - n_dropped_solve
  attr(out, "cv_factor")       <- cv_factor
  out
}

beta_G_tbl <- purrr::imap_dfr(post_main, function(p, pop) {
  fec_raw <- pop_data[[pop]]$fp$fec
  cv_fec  <- sd(fec_raw, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(fec_raw, na.rm = TRUE)
  bG <- beta_genetic_posterior(p$G_array,
                               fec_index = which(TRAITS == "fec_z"),
                               cv_factor = cv_fec)
  hpds <- apply(bG, 2, safe_hpd)
  tibble(
    Pop            = pop,
    trait          = colnames(bG),
    cv_fec         = cv_fec,
    beta_G_median  = apply(bG, 2, median, na.rm = TRUE),
    beta_G_mean    = colMeans(bG, na.rm = TRUE),
    beta_G_l95     = hpds[1, ],
    beta_G_u95     = hpds[2, ],
    n_kept         = attr(bG, "n_kept"),
    n_dropped      = attr(bG, "n_total") - attr(bG, "n_kept"),
    sig            = (hpds[1, ] > 0) | (hpds[2, ] < 0)
  )
})
beta_G_tbl
```

`cv_fec` shows the per-population rescaling factor — useful as a sanity
check, since β_G HPD widths scale linearly with it. `beta_G_median`
summarises the posterior because its distribution is heavy-tailed even
when **G**_zz is numerically non-singular: the `rcond(G_zz) < 1e-10`
guard rarely fires (see `n_dropped` ≈ 0 in practice), but moderately
ill-conditioned draws give large but finite values that pull the
posterior mean far from its central mass. The median is robust to these
tails; `beta_G_mean` is reported only for diagnostic comparison.

## 11.3 Side-by-side comparison plot

Filled symbols mark gradients whose 95% CI / HPD excludes zero.

```{r beta-comparison-plot, fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
# Per-population n from β_P (n is constant across traits within a pop after
# listwise deletion). Used to annotate the y-axis so BB's n=36 is visible.
n_by_pop <- beta_P_tbl %>%
  group_by(Pop) %>%
  summarise(n = max(n, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(pop_label = paste0(Pop, " (n=", n, ")"))

plot_dat <- bind_rows(
  beta_P_tbl %>%
    transmute(Pop, trait = term,
              mean = estimate, l95 = conf.low, u95 = conf.high,
              type = "Phenotypic β (fecundity)"),
  beta_G_tbl %>%
    transmute(Pop, trait,
              mean = beta_G_median, l95 = beta_G_l95, u95 = beta_G_u95,
              type = "Genetic β_G")
) %>%
  left_join(n_by_pop %>% select(Pop, pop_label), by = "Pop") %>%
  mutate(
    sig = (l95 > 0) | (u95 < 0),
    trait = recode_factor(trait,
              corolla_z = "corolla", SLA_z = "SLA",
              d13C_z    = "δ13C",    msm_z = "msm")
  )

ggplot(plot_dat, aes(mean, pop_label, colour = type, shape = sig)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = l95, xmax = u95),
                 height = 0.2, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  facet_wrap(~ trait, scales = "free_x", nrow = 1) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("FALSE" = 1, "TRUE" = 16),
                     labels = c("NS", "HPD excludes 0")) +
  labs(x = "Standardised selection gradient",
       y = NULL, colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**Figure 4.** Side-by-side comparison of phenotypic (β_P) and genetic
(β_G) selection gradients on z-scored traits, one panel per non-fitness
trait (corolla, SLA, δ¹³C, msm). Points are posterior medians (β_G) or
OLS estimates (β_P); error bars are 95% HPD intervals (β_G) or HC3 95%
CIs (β_P). Filled symbols mark gradients whose interval excludes zero;
open symbols are non-significant. Y-axis labels include the
complete-case n per population.

# 12 · Sibship-level associations between focal-plant traits and segment survival

The phenotypic β in §11 only sees plants that survived to flowering, so
it can't measure viability selection on the missing dead plants. Trait
data are only available on the F-plant (the designated focal sib, or
the first surviving substitute), so we cannot fit an individual-level
viability gradient. Instead we fit a segment-level binomial GLM
relating the F-plant's traits to the fraction of its segment-mates that
survived. **This is a sibship-level association, not a Lande viability
gradient**: a positive coefficient means segments whose surviving focal
sib happened to have a high trait value also had higher overall
survival, which can arise from family-mean trait differences correlated
with family-mean survival rather than from individual selection on that
trait. We report it as a descriptive complement to §11 and discuss the
distinction in §14.6. Coefficients should not be compared to published
β_v values from individual-level data.

## 12.1 Safety: cap survival counts at seeds sown

Survival counts come from `group_by(segment_id) %>% sum(surv_to_flower)`.
If, for any reason, the count ever exceeds `seeds_sown` (8 or 10
depending on population), something upstream is broken — most likely the
segment key. We cap silently but **warn loudly** so problems can't pass
unnoticed.

```{r cap-seeds-fn}
cap_seeds <- function(df, seeds_sown_val, pop_label) {
  n_over <- sum(df$total_surv_to_flower > seeds_sown_val, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (n_over > 0)
    warning(pop_label, ": ", n_over,
            " row(s) had total_surv_to_flower > seeds_sown and were capped")
  df$total_surv_to_flower <- pmin(df$total_surv_to_flower, seeds_sown_val)
  df
}
```

## 12.2 Segment-level survival GLM (sibship-level associations)

Quasi-binomial because survival counts are overdispersed (see §12.3).
The predictor side uses only the four non-fitness traits. Coefficients
are **trait-of-surviving-focal-sib × segment-survival-fraction**
associations, not individual viability gradients.

**Table 22.** Segment-level survival GLM per population: quasi-binomial
regression of `cbind(total_surv_to_flower, seeds_sown −
total_surv_to_flower)` on z-scored corolla, SLA, δ¹³C, and msm.
Columns from `broom::tidy()` give the coefficient estimate, SE,
z-statistic, p-value, and 95% CI. Trait values come from the surviving
focal sib, so these are sibship-level associations rather than
individual Lande viability gradients (see §14.6). Quasi-binomial family
used because of overdispersion documented in Table 23.

```{r surv-glm}
surv_summary <- purrr::imap_dfr(pop_data, function(prep, pop) {
  cfg <- POP_CONFIG[[pop]]
  d <- cap_seeds(prep$fp, cfg$seeds_sown, pop) %>%
    mutate(seeds_sown = cfg$seeds_sown) %>%
    select(total_surv_to_flower, seeds_sown,
           corolla_z, SLA_z, d13C_z, msm_z) %>%
    drop_na()
  if (nrow(d) < 10) return(NULL)
  mod <- glm(cbind(total_surv_to_flower, seeds_sown - total_surv_to_flower) ~
               corolla_z + SLA_z + d13C_z + msm_z,
             family = quasibinomial, data = d)
  broom::tidy(mod, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
    mutate(Pop = pop, .before = 1)
})
surv_summary
```

## 12.3 Overdispersion diagnostic

Pearson-residual dispersion (Σ rᵖ² / df) — values >> 1 justify the
quasi-binomial choice. The original analysis used quasi-binomial for BO
and HR for precisely this reason.

**Table 23.** Survival GLM overdispersion diagnostic per population:
the Pearson-residual dispersion statistic Σ rᵖ² / df. Values
substantially > 1 indicate binomial overdispersion and justify the
quasi-binomial family used in Table 22.

```{r surv-overdisp}
overdisp_fun <- function(model) {
  rp <- residuals(model, type = "pearson")
  sum(rp^2) / df.residual(model)
}

overdisp_tbl <- purrr::imap_dfr(pop_data, function(prep, pop) {
  cfg <- POP_CONFIG[[pop]]
  d <- cap_seeds(prep$fp, cfg$seeds_sown, pop) %>%
    mutate(seeds_sown = cfg$seeds_sown) %>%
    select(total_surv_to_flower, seeds_sown,
           corolla_z, SLA_z, d13C_z, msm_z) %>%
    drop_na()
  if (nrow(d) < 10) return(NULL)
  mod_binom <- glm(
    cbind(total_surv_to_flower, seeds_sown - total_surv_to_flower) ~
      corolla_z + SLA_z + d13C_z + msm_z,
    family = binomial, data = d)
  tibble(Pop = pop,
         overdispersion_ratio = overdisp_fun(mod_binom),
         family_used = "quasibinomial")
})
overdisp_tbl
```

# 13 · Sensitivity analyses

Three checks, in increasing breadth: (1) likelihood mis-specification on
fecundity (AC only); (2) trait drop / imputation reliance (BB only, where
missingness is highest); (3) prior mis-specification (AC and BB, the
most-complete and the most-vulnerable populations).

## 13.1 log1p(fec) sensitivity for β_G — likelihood specification

Refit AC with `log1p(fec)` z-scored as the fecundity column. Each
spec's β_G is rescaled to its own relative-fitness scale (CV of fec for
the raw spec, CV of log1p(fec) for the log spec) so both rows are
directly comparable as Lande gradients. If β_G is stable across the
two specs the Gaussian-on-raw-counts approximation is defensible; if it
shifts materially, prefer the log1p specification (or move to a Poisson
family in MCMCglmm).

**Table 24.** β_G sensitivity to fecundity likelihood specification at
AC, both rows on the Lande relative-fitness scale. The main analysis
(`spec = "raw fec (main)"`) uses `fec_z` from raw counts rescaled by
CV(fec); the refit (`spec = "log1p(fec) sensitivity"`) uses `fec_z`
from `log1p(fec)` rescaled by CV(log1p(fec)). Posterior medians
reported. Stable β_G across specs supports the Gaussian-on-raw-counts
approximation; large shifts would argue for a log or Poisson
likelihood.

```{r beta-genetic-fec-sensitivity}
prep_AC_logfec <- pop_data$AC
prep_AC_logfec$fp <- prep_AC_logfec$fp %>%
  mutate(fec_z = as.numeric(scale(log1p(fec))))

fits_logfec_AC <- cache_fit("fits_logfec_AC",
  fit_animal_model(prep_AC_logfec, peds_list$AC, prior_type = "px"))
post_logfec_AC <- extract_pop(fits_logfec_AC)

cv_log_AC <- with(prep_AC_logfec$fp,
                  sd(log1p(fec), na.rm = TRUE) /
                  mean(log1p(fec), na.rm = TRUE))

bG_logfec_AC <- beta_genetic_posterior(post_logfec_AC$G_array,
                                       fec_index = which(TRAITS == "fec_z"),
                                       cv_factor = cv_log_AC)
hpd_logfec <- apply(bG_logfec_AC, 2, safe_hpd)

beta_G_fec_compare <- bind_rows(
  beta_G_tbl %>%
    filter(Pop == "AC") %>%
    transmute(trait,
              beta_G = beta_G_median, l95 = beta_G_l95, u95 = beta_G_u95,
              spec   = "raw fec (main)"),
  tibble(trait  = colnames(bG_logfec_AC),
         beta_G = apply(bG_logfec_AC, 2, median, na.rm = TRUE),
         l95    = hpd_logfec[1, ], u95 = hpd_logfec[2, ],
         spec   = "log1p(fec) sensitivity")
)
beta_G_fec_compare
```

## 13.2 BB trait-drop sensitivity — imputation reliance

BB has the highest missingness (SLA 69%, msm 75%). Its five-trait r_A
estimates depend partly on MCMCglmm's multivariate-normal imputation
rather than directly observed data. We refit BB twice — once dropping SLA,
once dropping msm — and compare the surviving r_A entries against the
five-trait posterior. Stable estimates ⇒ data-driven; large shifts or
sign flips ⇒ imputation-driven.

### 13.2.1 Subset-trait refit function

A trimmed version of `fit_animal_model` that takes a `traits_keep`
argument and rebuilds the prior at the matching dimension.

```{r bb-subset-fn}
fit_animal_model_subset <- function(prep, peds, traits_keep,
                                    nitt = NITT, burnin = BURNIN, thin = THIN,
                                    n_chains = N_CHAINS) {
  nt_k <- length(traits_keep)
  dat  <- as.data.frame(prep$fp)
  Ainv <- peds$Ainv
  dat$animal <- factor(trimws(as.character(dat$animal)),
                       levels = rownames(Ainv))
  dat$animal     <- droplevels(dat$animal)
  dat$dam        <- factor(dat$dam)
  dat$block      <- factor(dat$block)
  dat$transect_f <- factor(dat$transect_f)

  prior <- list(
    G = list(
      G1 = list(V = diag(nt_k), nu = nt_k, alpha.mu = rep(0, nt_k),
                alpha.V = diag(nt_k) * 1000),  # animal
      G2 = list(V = diag(nt_k), nu = nt_k, alpha.mu = rep(0, nt_k),
                alpha.V = diag(nt_k) * 1000),  # dam
      G3 = list(V = diag(nt_k), nu = nt_k, alpha.mu = rep(0, nt_k),
                alpha.V = diag(nt_k) * 1000),  # block (PX, matches main)
      G4 = list(V = diag(nt_k), nu = nt_k, alpha.mu = rep(0, nt_k),
                alpha.V = diag(nt_k) * 1000)   # transect (PX, matches main)
    ),
    R = list(V = diag(nt_k), nu = nt_k)
  )

  lhs     <- paste0("cbind(", paste(traits_keep, collapse = ", "), ")")
  fixed_f <- as.formula(paste(lhs, "~ trait - 1"))

  fit_one <- function(seed) {
    set.seed(seed)
    MCMCglmm(
      fixed    = fixed_f,
      random   = ~ us(trait):animal + us(trait):dam
                 + idh(trait):block + idh(trait):transect_f,
      rcov     = ~ us(trait):units,
      family   = rep("gaussian", nt_k),
      ginverse = list(animal = Ainv),
      data     = dat,
      prior    = prior,
      nitt     = nitt, burnin = burnin, thin = thin,
      verbose  = FALSE
    )
  }
  purrr::map(seq_len(n_chains), fit_one)
}

extract_rA_subset <- function(fits, traits_keep) {
  VCV  <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, function(f) as.matrix(f$VCV)))
  nt_k <- length(traits_keep)
  G_arr <- array(NA_real_, dim = c(nrow(VCV), nt_k, nt_k),
                 dimnames = list(NULL, traits_keep, traits_keep))
  for (i in seq_along(traits_keep)) for (j in seq_along(traits_keep)) {
    G_arr[, i, j] <- VCV[, paste0("trait", traits_keep[i], ":trait",
                                  traits_keep[j], ".animal")]
  }
  rA_arr <- array(NA_real_, dim = dim(G_arr), dimnames = dimnames(G_arr))
  for (k in seq_len(dim(G_arr)[1])) rA_arr[k, , ] <- cov2cor_mat(G_arr[k, , ])
  rA_arr
}
```

### 13.2.2 Run BB without SLA and without msm

```{r bb-subset-fits}
traits_no_SLA <- setdiff(TRAITS, "SLA_z")
traits_no_msm <- setdiff(TRAITS, "msm_z")

fits_BB_no_SLA <- cache_fit("fits_BB_no_SLA",
  fit_animal_model_subset(pop_data$BB, peds_list$BB, traits_no_SLA))
fits_BB_no_msm <- cache_fit("fits_BB_no_msm",
  fit_animal_model_subset(pop_data$BB, peds_list$BB, traits_no_msm))

rA_BB_main   <- post_main$BB$rA_array
rA_BB_no_SLA <- extract_rA_subset(fits_BB_no_SLA, traits_no_SLA)
rA_BB_no_msm <- extract_rA_subset(fits_BB_no_msm, traits_no_msm)
```

### 13.2.3 Compare overlapping r_A entries

`delta` is the per-pair shift in posterior mean (subset − main). A
well-conditioned five-trait fit should show `max_abs_delta < 0.1`,
`n_HPD_nonoverlap = 0`, and no sign changes.

**Table 25.** BB trait-drop sensitivity for genetic correlations.
`rA_BB_sensitivity` (first printed table) gives per-pair r_A under the
main five-trait fit vs. the drop-SLA and drop-msm refits, with HPD
bounds and `delta = rA_sub − rA_main`. `rA_BB_sens_summary` (second
table) reports per-spec totals: number of overlapping pairs, max and
median |Δ|, HPD-non-overlap count, and sign-change count.

```{r bb-subset-compare}
compare_rA <- function(rA_main, rA_sub, traits_sub, label) {
  ut <- which(upper.tri(diag(length(traits_sub))), arr.ind = TRUE)
  purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(ut)), function(idx) {
    i  <- ut[idx, 1]; j <- ut[idx, 2]
    t1 <- traits_sub[i]; t2 <- traits_sub[j]
    x_main <- rA_main[, t1, t2]
    x_sub  <- rA_sub[, i, j]
    h_main <- safe_hpd(x_main); h_sub <- safe_hpd(x_sub)
    tibble(spec        = label,
           trait1      = t1, trait2 = t2,
           rA_main     = mean(x_main, na.rm = TRUE),
           rA_main_l95 = h_main[1], rA_main_u95 = h_main[2],
           rA_sub      = mean(x_sub,  na.rm = TRUE),
           rA_sub_l95  = h_sub[1],   rA_sub_u95  = h_sub[2],
           delta       = mean(x_sub, na.rm = TRUE) -
                         mean(x_main, na.rm = TRUE))
  })
}

rA_BB_sensitivity <- bind_rows(
  compare_rA(rA_BB_main, rA_BB_no_SLA, traits_no_SLA, "drop SLA"),
  compare_rA(rA_BB_main, rA_BB_no_msm, traits_no_msm, "drop msm")
)
rA_BB_sensitivity

rA_BB_sens_summary <- rA_BB_sensitivity %>%
  group_by(spec) %>%
  summarise(
    n_pairs          = n(),
    max_abs_delta    = max(abs(delta), na.rm = TRUE),
    median_abs_delta = median(abs(delta), na.rm = TRUE),
    n_HPD_nonoverlap = sum(rA_main_u95 < rA_sub_l95
                           | rA_sub_u95 < rA_main_l95, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_sign_change    = sum(sign(rA_main) != sign(rA_sub), na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
rA_BB_sens_summary
```

## 13.3 Prior sensitivity (PX vs IW) — AC and BB

Three sets of quantities are compared between the PX and IW priors:

- **r_A** (genetic correlations) — the original check.
- **V_A diagonals** — prior sensitivity here would indicate that
  heritability estimates are prior-dominated.
- **V_M diagonals** — with only ~3 full-sibs per dam, V_M is weakly
  identified and the most likely place to see a prior-driven shift.

### 13.3.1 Extraction helper covering all three quantities

```{r prior-sensitivity-fn}
extract_prior_sensitivity <- function(fits) {
  VCV      <- combine_VCV(fits)
  G_array  <- build_G_array(VCV, "animal")
  M_array  <- build_G_array(VCV, "dam")
  rA_array <- rA_from_G(G_array)

  s_rA <- posterior_summary_matrix(rA_array)
  rA_tbl <- tibble(
    quantity = paste0("rA_",
                      outer(TRAITS, TRAITS, paste, sep = "/")[upper.tri(diag(NT))]),
    mean = s_rA$mean[upper.tri(s_rA$mean)],
    l95  = s_rA$l95[upper.tri(s_rA$l95)],
    u95  = s_rA$u95[upper.tri(s_rA$u95)]
  )

  Va_draws <- sapply(seq_len(NT), function(i) G_array[, i, i])
  Va_tbl <- tibble(
    quantity = paste0("Va_", TRAITS),
    mean = colMeans(Va_draws, na.rm = TRUE),
    l95  = apply(Va_draws, 2, function(x) safe_hpd(x)[1]),
    u95  = apply(Va_draws, 2, function(x) safe_hpd(x)[2])
  )

  Vm_draws <- sapply(seq_len(NT), function(i) M_array[, i, i])
  Vm_tbl <- tibble(
    quantity = paste0("Vm_", TRAITS),
    mean = colMeans(Vm_draws, na.rm = TRUE),
    l95  = apply(Vm_draws, 2, function(x) safe_hpd(x)[1]),
    u95  = apply(Vm_draws, 2, function(x) safe_hpd(x)[2])
  )

  bind_rows(rA_tbl, Va_tbl, Vm_tbl)
}
```

### 13.3.2 Long-format comparison

**Table 26.** Prior sensitivity (long format) comparing the
parameter-expanded (PX, main) and inverse-Wishart (IW, V = I, ν = NT)
priors at AC and BB. One row per quantity: 10 r_A entries, 5 V_A
diagonals, and 5 V_M diagonals per population × prior combination.
Columns give posterior mean and 95% HPD bounds.

```{r prior-sensitivity-long}
ac_px <- extract_prior_sensitivity(fits_main$AC) %>%
  mutate(Pop = "AC", prior = "PX (default)")
ac_iw <- extract_prior_sensitivity(fits_iw_AC) %>%
  mutate(Pop = "AC", prior = "IW(V=I, nu=nt)")

bb_px <- extract_prior_sensitivity(fits_main$BB) %>%
  mutate(Pop = "BB", prior = "PX (default)")
bb_iw <- extract_prior_sensitivity(fits_iw_BB) %>%
  mutate(Pop = "BB", prior = "IW(V=I, nu=nt)")

prior_compare <- bind_rows(ac_px, ac_iw, bb_px, bb_iw) %>%
  select(Pop, prior, quantity, mean, l95, u95)
prior_compare
```

### 13.3.3 Wide format with `delta_mean` and HPD-overlap flag

**Table 27.** Prior sensitivity (wide format) pivoted so each row
gives one quantity with PX and IW posterior means and HPDs side by
side, the difference `delta_mean = IW − PX`, and `hpd_overlap` (TRUE
when the two priors' 95% HPDs overlap; FALSE flags prior-sensitive
quantities).

```{r prior-sensitivity-wide}
prior_compare_wide <- prior_compare %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = prior,
              values_from = c(mean, l95, u95),
              names_glue = "{prior}_{.value}") %>%
  mutate(
    delta_mean = `IW(V=I, nu=nt)_mean` - `PX (default)_mean`,
    hpd_overlap = !(`PX (default)_u95` < `IW(V=I, nu=nt)_l95` |
                    `IW(V=I, nu=nt)_u95` < `PX (default)_l95`)
  ) %>%
  arrange(Pop, quantity)
prior_compare_wide
```

# 14 · Limitations and constraints on interpretation

Several features of the design and posterior structure constrain which
inferences this analysis supports. They are documented here so the strength
of each Results claim can be weighed against them.

## 14.1 Sampling design limits resolution of off-diagonal **G**

Each population is sampled at ~40–49 sires, ~3 dams per sire, and ~3
F-plants per dam (Table 03_sample_sizes). With this design, Falconer's
approximation gives SE(*h*²) ≈ 2/√(n_dams × n_off/dam) ≈ 0.10–0.12 per
trait — sufficient to resolve heritabilities of *h*² ≳ 0.3 but not lower.
The same data must support 10 off-diagonal entries in each 5 × 5 **G**, and
the posteriors confirm the resulting power limit: only 1 of 40 pairwise
*r*_A values has an HPD that excludes zero (HR δ¹³C × mean seed mass,
*r*_A = 0.58 [0.25, 0.87]). The remaining 39 span roughly [−0.8, +0.8],
meaning the data cannot distinguish strong positive from strong negative
correlations. Comparisons of **G** structure across populations (Random
Skewers, eigenanalysis, β_G) operate on this floor of resolution.

## 14.2 Variance components are prior-sensitive in posterior mean

The PX/IW comparison in §13.3 (Table 13_sensitivity_prior_wide) shows
two kinds of prior sensitivity. **Strict HPD non-overlap** is the
narrow case — fewer rows than the manuscript narrative might suggest:
only Va_fec_z at BB (1 of 5 V_A entries), Vm_corolla_z and Vm_fec_z at
BB (2 of 5 V_M entries), Va_SLA_z at AC (1 of 5), and Vm_SLA_z,
Vm_corolla_z, Vm_fec_z at AC (3 of 5). **Posterior-mean shifts**
between priors are more pervasive: IW(V = I, ν = NT = 5) is improper at
this dimension (its mean does not exist for ν ≤ NT + 1) and pulls
posterior means toward V = I, so IW means are systematically larger
than PX means even where their wide HPDs overlap — at BB, V_A means
shift 2–7× between priors for every trait. We adopt PX as the main
analysis because it is the appropriate weakly-informative prior for
variance components with few random-effect levels (Gelman 2006) and
because IW(V = I, ν = NT) is improper here. **Defensible claim**:
δ¹³C V_A at HR and AC, and mean seed mass V_A at HR, have lower HPDs
clearly above zero under both priors and posterior-mean shifts < 2×.
All other reported V_A and V_M values should be read as posterior
summaries under the PX prior rather than data-driven point estimates.
We avoid claims about heritability magnitude per §14.8.

## 14.3 Genetic selection gradients β_G are precision-limited

The Robertson–Price identity is the right object for predicting
evolutionary change, but its precision is bounded by that of off-diagonal
**G**. None of 16 β_G estimates has an HPD that excludes zero, and HPD
widths span 1.5–10 standardised units. We protect against occasional
near-singular **G**_zz draws via `rcond(G_zz) < 1e-10` exclusion and report
posterior medians rather than means (§11.2). Even with these fixes the β_G
intervals are too wide to test alignment with β_P or with environmental
predictors. β_G results are best read as confirming no clear conflict with
β_P given available precision, not as positive evidence of alignment.

## 14.4 BB phenotypic selection is underpowered

After listwise deletion, β_P at BB rests on n = 36 complete cases
(corolla, SLA, δ¹³C, msm, fec all non-missing) versus n = 185 at AC, 62 at
BO, 296 at HR (Table 11_beta_P_fit_summary). The marginal global *F* and
individual coefficient significance for BB are largely small-sample
artefacts and should be read alongside the n column.

## 14.5 Inference is conditional on survival

Trait values are measured only on F-plants — individuals that survived to
flowering. Where no designated F-plant survived in a segment, the first
surviving sibling was substituted; segments with no survivors enter the
fitness regression with W = 0 but contribute no trait data. The **G**
matrices estimated here are therefore **post-viability-selection G**, not
the parental **G** that determines next-generation response. If viability
selection acts on the same traits, our **G** systematically understates
pre-selection genetic variance and the implied response to fecundity
selection.

## 14.6 The viability GLM is a sibship-level analysis

Because F-plants are themselves survivors (or the first row in all-dead
segments), the binomial GLM regressing segment-level survival counts on
F-plant traits is not a Lande viability gradient. It asks whether the
surviving focal sib's trait predicts the survival fraction of the whole
segment — a sibship-level association, not individual viability selection.
This is the closest substitute possible given the protocol (no traits were
measured pre-mortality); it should be reported accordingly.

## 14.7 Other constraints

- **PC2 is unreliable in all four populations** (Table 08_pc2_reliability).
  λ₂ and λ₃ HPDs overlap at every site, so PC2 eigenvectors are not
  stably identified across draws. Only PC1 contributions are interpreted.

- **Block variance is weakly identified from three levels.** With three
  blocks per site, V_block carries little information from the data. An
  earlier version of the model used a near-improper inverse-Gamma-like
  prior (`nu = 0.002`) on the block component, which produced R̂ > 1.2 for
  five HR block parameters. The current PX prior on `idh(trait):block`
  (and on `idh(trait):transect_f`) — `nu = NT`, `alpha.V = 1000·I` —
  **substantially reduces but does not eliminate** the mixing
  pathology: per Table 05_convergence_rhat_above_1_1, 15 parameters
  across the four populations still have R̂ > 1.1 and 9 have R̂ > 1.2,
  almost all of them block-related. The PX prior follows Gelman (2006)
  for variance components with few random-effect levels and is the
  appropriate weakly-informative choice, but the fundamental
  identifiability issue remains: V_block cannot be precisely estimated
  from three random levels regardless of prior. Block remains in the
  model as a necessary nuisance term so that V_block is not absorbed
  into V_A or V_R, but V_block itself is not reported as a target
  quantity and the elevated R̂ values for block parameters should not be
  taken as evidence against the V_A and *r*_A estimates the block
  effect protects.

- **BB depends heavily on multivariate-normal imputation.** SLA, msm, and
  δ¹³C are 49–75% missing at BB. The trait-drop sensitivity in §13.2
  shows surviving *r*_A entries shift by at most 0.025 when SLA or msm is
  omitted, providing some reassurance that the 5-trait **G** is not driven
  by imputation artefacts — but it does not validate the imputed values
  themselves.

## 14.8 Defensible inferences from these data

Taking the constraints above together:

1. **Appreciable additive genetic variance (V_A) in δ¹³C and mean seed
   mass at HR, and δ¹³C at AC.** Posterior means and lower HPD bounds:
   HR δ¹³C V_A = 0.45 [0.24, 0.68]; HR mean seed mass V_A = 0.32 [0.07,
   0.57]; AC δ¹³C V_A = 0.42 [0.12, 0.72]. These three are the V_A
   estimates whose lower HPDs sit clearly above zero under the PX prior
   and whose posterior means change less than 2× between PX and IW. We
   report these as **V_A** rather than as heritabilities because
   per-draw *h*² = V_A / (V_A + V_M + V_block + V_transect + V_R) has a
   highly variable denominator under the wide PX prior on every
   variance component, so *h*² lower HPDs touch zero even when V_A is
   well-resolved (Table 06_h2_narrow_sense versus Table
   06_Va_diagonals). Posterior-mean *h*² for these three is 0.25–0.28,
   but lower HPD bounds are essentially zero; the defensible biological
   claim is the presence of heritable variation, not a specific *h*²
   magnitude.

2. **A credible additive genetic correlation between δ¹³C and mean seed
   mass at HR** (*r*_A = 0.58, HPD [0.27, 0.88]; the only one of 40
   pairwise *r*_A entries whose HPD excludes zero).

3. **Phenotypic selection patterns at AC and HR** favouring more negative
   δ¹³C and lower mean seed mass. β_P at AC has n = 185 and significant
   HC3 coefficients for both δ¹³C and msm; HR has n = 296 and a similar
   pattern.

4. **BB and BO are essentially unpowered** for selection and **G**-matrix
   structure inferences and should be reported as such.

5. **No credible evidence** for or against alignment of β_P with β_G in
   any population — even after rescaling β_G to the relative-fitness
   scale (§11.2), the intervals are too wide to test alignment.

These are the claims the data currently support. The Rmd documents
everything else (full **G** matrices, eigenanalyses, evolvability metrics,
Random Skewers, full β_P/β_G tables, prior sensitivity) so reviewers can
assess them against the limitations above.

# 15 · Save tables to disk

Every named table referenced in the document is written here to `tables/`
as a CSV. Figures are written to `figures/` automatically via the
`fig.path` chunk option set in the setup block (top of file).

```{r save-outputs}
save_tbl <- function(x, name) {
  if (is.null(x)) return(invisible(NULL))
  readr::write_csv(x, file.path("tables", paste0(name, ".csv")))
}

# Section 3 — data + sample sizes
save_tbl(sample_sizes,       "03_sample_sizes")
save_tbl(missingness_tbl,    "03_missingness_per_trait")
save_tbl(trait_means_tbl,    "03_raw_trait_means")

# Section 5 — convergence
save_tbl(conv_health,                       "05_convergence_rhat_health")
save_tbl(conv_tbl %>% filter(psrf > 1.1)
                  %>% arrange(desc(psrf)),  "05_convergence_rhat_above_1_1")
save_tbl(ess_health,                        "05_convergence_ess_health")
save_tbl(ess_tbl  %>% arrange(ESS)
                  %>% head(20),             "05_convergence_ess_lowest20")

# Section 6 — variance components and heritability
save_tbl(Va_tbl, "06_Va_diagonals")
save_tbl(Vm_tbl, "06_Vm_diagonals")
save_tbl(h2_tbl, "06_h2_narrow_sense")

# Section 7 — genetic correlations
save_tbl(rA_pairs_tbl, "07_rA_pairs")

# Section 8 — eigenanalysis
save_tbl(eig_summary_tbl,  "08_eigen_summary")
save_tbl(pc2_reliable_tbl, "08_pc2_reliability")
save_tbl(pc1_loadings_tbl, "08_pc1_loadings")
save_tbl(pc2_loadings_tbl, "08_pc2_loadings")
save_tbl(pc1_contrib_str,  "08_pc1_contributors")
save_tbl(pc2_contrib_str,  "08_pc2_contributors")

# Section 9 — evolvability
save_tbl(evol_tbl,      "09_evolvability_metrics")
save_tbl(evol_wide_tbl, "09_evolvability_metrics_wide")

# Section 10 — Random Skewers
save_tbl(rs_tbl, "10_random_skewers")

# Section 11 — selection
save_tbl(beta_P_tbl,         "11_beta_P_fec_only")
save_tbl(beta_P_total,       "11_beta_P_total_fitness")
save_tbl(beta_P_all,         "11_beta_P_combined")
save_tbl(beta_P_fit_summary, "11_beta_P_fit_summary")

# Section 12 — viability

        " CSV files to tables/, ",
        length(list.files("figures", pattern = "\\.png$")),
```
